title: Dune
subtitle: Frank Herbert, 1965
blurb: Young Paul Atreides is thrust into the treacherous politics of Arrakis — the desert planet and sole source of the universe-controlling spice melange — after his noble house is betrayed and destroyed. Forced to survive among the indigenous Fremen, Paul transforms into the messianic Muad'Dib and leads a revolution that topples an empire. Herbert's novel is simultaneously an epic of heroic ascent and a cautionary warning about the catastrophic cost of superheroes.
setting_preamble: The novel is set in a feudal interstellar civilization controlled by a Padishah Emperor and competing noble Houses. Interstellar travel is monopolized by the Spacing Guild, whose Navigators require the spice melange to fold space. Melange grows only on Arrakis (Dune) and is the most valuable substance in the universe. The Bene Gesserit Sisterhood runs a millennia-long secret breeding program aimed at producing a superbeing called the Kwisatz Haderach — a male who can bridge space and time through prescience. Mentats are humans conditioned to perform computer-like logical analysis, since thinking machines are forbidden. The Fremen are the native desert people of Arrakis, shaped by scarcity into fearsome warriors, secretly guided toward terraforming their world.

factions.label: House Atreides
factions.description: Noble house of Duke Leto, rulers of Caladan and reluctant stewards of Arrakis; renowned for their honorable reputation and well-trained military, which the Emperor secretly fears as a threat to his throne.

factions.label: House Harkonnen
factions.description: Cruel and cunning rival house to the Atreides; previous rulers of Arrakis and co-conspirators with the Emperor in the destruction of House Atreides. Left politically defunct by the novel's end.

factions.label: Fremen
factions.description: Indigenous desert people of Arrakis, hardened by scarcity into peerless warriors; harbor a Bene Gesserit-seeded messianic prophecy that Paul exploits to build his revolutionary army.

factions.label: Bene Gesserit Sisterhood
factions.description: Ancient order of women trained in physical and mental disciplines; run a centuries-long covert eugenics breeding program aimed at producing the Kwisatz Haderach, and have seeded messianic myths among Fremen populations through their Missionaria Protectiva.

factions.label: Imperial House Corrino
factions.description: The ruling dynasty under Padishah Emperor Shaddam IV, whose Sardaukar super-soldiers and secret alliance with the Harkonnens sustain his grip on power — until Paul's control of the spice forces his abdication.

factions.label: Arrakis Smugglers
factions.description: Independent spice-running operation on Arrakis, operating in the margins between Imperial law and Harkonnen control; Gurney Halleck takes refuge with them after the fall of House Atreides.

characters.name: Paul Atreides
characters.role: Heir of House Atreides; Fremen Muad'Dib; revolutionary leader
characters.description: Trained in both Bene Gesserit disciplines and Mentat logic, Paul's ultimate power — prescience — transcends both systems and becomes a cage rather than a gift. His victory over the Emperor is simultaneously a liberation and the conscious unleashing of a galaxy-wide jihad he foresees and chooses not to prevent, making him, in Herbert's framing, a catastrophe as much as a hero.
characters.name_evidence: protagonist; son of Duke Leto and Lady Jessica; becomes messianic leader of the Fremen

characters.name: Lady Jessica
characters.role: Bene Gesserit adept; Duke Leto's concubine; mother of Paul and Alia
characters.description: Jessica defied the Bene Gesserit's explicit instruction to produce a daughter and bore Paul out of love for Leto — a seemingly personal act that derailed the Sisterhood's centuries-long breeding program. Her complicity in the Missionaria Protectiva's exploitation of Fremen culture, and her own transformation into a Fremen Reverend Mother, make her both a victim of and a participant in the novel's larger systems of manipulation.
characters.name_evidence: concubine of Duke Leto; Bene Gesserit sister who defied Sisterhood's orders by bearing a son

characters.name: Duke Leto Atreides I
characters.role: Duke of House Atreides; ruler of Arrakis
characters.description: Leto accepts the poisoned gift of Arrakis knowing it is a trap, judging that refusal would mean war — a tragic bind between honorable duty and political suicide. His death by Yueh's betrayal and the Baron's poison gas is the catalytic event of the novel, yet his lineage, unknowingly carrying Harkonnen blood, ultimately inherits the empire he died trying to serve.
characters.name_evidence: head of House Atreides; ruler of Caladan, then reluctant governor of Arrakis

characters.name: Baron Vladimir Harkonnen
characters.role: Head of House Harkonnen; primary antagonist
characters.description: The novel's chief villain is also its supreme ironic figure: the Baron's genetic legacy secretly pervades the very dynasty that destroys him, since he is Jessica's secret father and therefore Paul and Alia's grandfather. He is killed not by Paul but by the four-year-old Alia, who whispers the revelation of her lineage to him as she administers the gom jabbar.
characters.name_evidence: cunning and cruel leader of House Harkonnen; unbeknownst to her, father of Lady Jessica

characters.name: Feyd-Rautha Harkonnen
characters.role: Harkonnen heir and gladiator; Kwisatz Haderach candidate
characters.description: Feyd-Rautha is simultaneously the Baron's chosen successor and, structurally, an alternate candidate for the Bene Gesserit's Kwisatz Haderach — the Sisterhood planned their own Harkonnen-Atreides union that would have made him or his offspring their hoped-for superbeing. Paul's ritual killing of him forecloses this possibility and consolidates the novel's resolution.
characters.name_evidence: younger nephew and heir of Baron Vladimir Harkonnen; the Baron's designated na-Baron

characters.name: Glossu "Beast" Rabban Harkonnen
characters.role: Harkonnen governor of Arrakis; instrument of deliberate cruelty
characters.description: Rabban is not simply cruel but instrumentally cruel — the Baron deploys his brutality as a calculated PR maneuver, knowing Rabban's oppression will make Feyd-Rautha's eventual replacement look merciful by contrast. He is killed in the early stages of the Battle of Arrakeen.
characters.name_evidence: older nephew of Baron Harkonnen; Baron places him in charge of Arrakis to be terrible to the people

characters.name: Piter de Vries
characters.role: Twisted Mentat; Baron's chief intelligence operative
characters.description: As the Baron's Mentat, Piter embodies reason weaponized entirely in the service of cruelty — he both engineered Yueh's betrayal and orchestrated the misdirection of Thufir Hawat toward suspecting Jessica. He is killed by the poison gas from Duke Leto's fake tooth before he can claim his promised reward of Lady Jessica.
characters.name_evidence: the Baron's twisted Mentat; broke Yueh's Suk Imperial Conditioning through torture of Yueh's wife

characters.name: Dr. Wellington Yueh
characters.role: Atreides physician; coerced traitor
characters.description: Yueh's betrayal is the novel's central dramatic shock precisely because his Suk School conditioning — a psychological guarantee against harm to patients — was supposed to make it impossible. His complicity is not villainy but broken loyalty under the unbearable duress of his wife Wanna's captivity and torture, which the novel frames as a systemic failure of the conditioning itself rather than simple moral weakness.
characters.name_evidence: the Atreides' doctor; betrays the Atreides to the Harkonnens; Suk School conditioning broken

characters.name: Thufir Hawat
characters.role: Atreides Master of Assassins; Mentat
characters.description: Hawat is the novel's case study in how reason itself can be weaponized against its user: his pride in his analytical abilities makes him susceptible to the Baron's planted misinformation, and his false conviction that Jessica is the traitor drives him into Harkonnen service. His death-by-choice at the novel's end — preferring suicide via Harkonnen poison to assassinating Paul — is both his redemption and Herbert's commentary on the limits of pure logic.
characters.name_evidence: powerful Mentat and Master of Assassins for House Atreides; guided by Harkonnens to suspect Jessica

characters.name: Gurney Halleck
characters.role: Atreides master-of-arms; warrior-poet
characters.description: Gurney escapes the Harkonnen attack and falls in with the Arrakis smugglers, becoming disillusioned before eventually reuniting with Paul. His suspicion of Jessica — shared with Hawat — illustrates how thoroughly the Harkonnens' misdirection campaign penetrated even the most loyal Atreides retainers.
characters.name_evidence: master-of-arms and one of Duke Leto's most trusted advisers; later joins the smugglers

characters.name: Duncan Idaho
characters.role: Atreides swordmaster; first Fremen contact
characters.description: Duncan's role as the bridge between House Atreides and the Fremen — making first contact with Stilgar's sietch — is cut short when he dies fighting a Harkonnen rearguard action to cover Paul and Jessica's escape. His death marks the end of the old Atreides world.
characters.name_evidence: Atreides swordmaster and ambassador to the Fremen; makes first contact with Stilgar's sietch

characters.name: Stilgar
characters.role: Naib (chief) of Sietch Tabr; Paul's key military commander
characters.description: Stilgar embodies Fremen pragmatism: he accepts Paul and Jessica not out of blind faith in prophecy but because their demonstrated skills make them worth absorbing into the sietch. His evolution from skeptical tribal leader to devoted general mirrors the broader Fremen transformation that Paul's arrival catalyzes.
characters.name_evidence: Fremen leader, naib of Sietch Tabr, uncle of Chani; accepts Paul and Jessica into Fremen society

characters.name: Chani
characters.role: Fremen warrior; Paul's companion and concubine
characters.description: Chani is Paul's true partner and the mother of his son Leto, who is killed in a Harkonnen raid. At the novel's close she accepts the political reality of Paul's marriage to Irulan without bitterness, and Jessica's final words reframe Chani as the one whom history will call wife — the novel's quiet assertion that love and power occupy different registers.
characters.name_evidence: Fremen warrior, daughter of Liet-Kynes and niece of Stilgar; Paul's lover; bears him a son

characters.name: Liet-Kynes
characters.role: Imperial Planetologist; secret Fremen leader
characters.description: Kynes occupies two completely contradictory roles — official Imperial functionary and secret architect of Fremen terraforming resistance — and his death in the desert exposes the fatal contradiction in his life's work: the ecological transformation he devoted himself to would destroy the sandworms and, with them, the spice that gives the Fremen their leverage. He is Herbert's clearest embodiment of idealism undermined by its own structural irony.
characters.name_evidence: Imperial planetologist and Judge of the Change; secretly Chani's father and secret leader of the Fremen

characters.name: Reverend Mother Gaius Helen Mohiam
characters.role: Bene Gesserit Reverend Mother; Emperor's Truthsayer
characters.description: Mohiam embodies the Bene Gesserit's fundamental hypocrisy: as Truthsayer she serves the Emperor while simultaneously running the Sisterhood's covert breeding agenda, and it was she who instructed Jessica to conceive a daughter — the order Jessica defied. At the novel's climax she compels Shaddam to capitulate to Paul, a final act that subordinates her Imperial loyalty to Bene Gesserit survival.
characters.name_evidence: the Emperor's Truthsayer; tests Paul with the gom jabbar; instructed to collect Baron's genetic material

characters.name: Alia Atreides
characters.role: Pre-born Reverend Mother; killer of Baron Harkonnen
characters.description: Alia's existence is an unintended consequence of Jessica's Water of Life ritual — the child in the womb received full Reverend Mother consciousness before birth, making her an 'Abomination' in Bene Gesserit terms and a figure of destabilizing power. At approximately four years old she poisons the Baron with a gom jabbar and reveals their family connection to him in his final moments, collapsing the novel's moral binary in a single act.
characters.name_evidence: Paul's sister; conscious awakening in the womb; born fully aware Reverend Mother; kills Baron Harkonnen

characters.name: Emperor Shaddam Corrino IV
characters.role: Padishah Emperor of the Known Universe
characters.description: Shaddam's secret co-conspiracy with the Harkonnens — lending his Sardaukar troops to their attack on House Atreides — is the novel's central political revelation, transforming what appeared to be a neutral administrative transfer of Arrakis into a state-sponsored assassination. Stripped of his Sardaukar advantage once Paul controls the spice, he capitulates entirely, a ruler who gambled the entire imperial order on a backstab and lost.
characters.name_evidence: the 81st Padishah Emperor; secretly aligned with Harkonnens; forced to abdicate by Paul

characters.name: Princess Irulan Corrino
characters.role: Imperial Princess; Paul's political wife; historian of Muad'Dib
characters.description: Irulan's most significant presence in the novel is structural rather than active — her fictional future writings frame every chapter as already-mythologized history, positioning the reader as a retrospective audience aware that Paul's story has become legend. She becomes Paul's political wife to legitimize his claim to the throne but will live, in Jessica's final words, as less than a concubine.
characters.name_evidence: the Emperor's eldest daughter; writes fictional books about Muad'Dib; each chapter begins with her epigraphs

characters.name: Count Hasimir Fenring
characters.role: Imperial assassin; Emperor's closest confidant
characters.description: Fenring is a near-miss of Paul's own nature — a failed Kwisatz Haderach who is invisible to Paul's prescient vision, making him the one person who might have killed Paul in the novel's climax. His refusal of the Emperor's order to do so is both a personal choice and a tacit acknowledgment of a kinship he shares with Paul as a product of the Bene Gesserit's breeding ambitions.
characters.name_evidence: trained killer and Mentat; genetic eunuch; failed Kwisatz Haderach attempt; refuses order to kill Paul

characters.name: Lady Margot Fenring
characters.role: Bene Gesserit operative; Count Fenring's wife
characters.description: Lady Margot's seduction of Feyd-Rautha is a Bene Gesserit insurance policy — by bearing his daughter she preserves the Harkonnen genetic line within the Sisterhood's breeding program even as Paul's victory renders it politically extinct. She is among the novel's clearest examples of the Bene Gesserit treating human beings as genetic assets.
characters.name_evidence: a beautiful Bene Gesserit sister; seduces Feyd-Rautha to preserve his bloodline

characters.name: Shadout Mapes
characters.role: Fremen household servant; Bene Gesserit identifier
characters.description: Mapes is the first Fremen character to interact with the Atreides household and the first to recognize Jessica's Bene Gesserit training, signaling that the Missionaria Protectiva's religious seeding has prepared Arrakis for exactly this encounter. She is killed during Yueh's betrayal.
characters.name_evidence: Fremen servant of the Atreides; first Fremen to test Jessica and discover she is Bene Gesserit

characters.name: Jamis
characters.role: Fremen warrior; Paul's first kill among the Fremen
characters.description: Jamis rejects the messianic framing of Paul's arrival and demands proof through ritual combat, forcing Paul to kill a man — and absorb the full cultural weight of Fremen death customs — as his initiation price. His challenge is the pivot point that transforms Paul from a fugitive refugee into a recognized member of Fremen society.
characters.name_evidence: Fremen warrior who challenges Paul to a fight to the death and is killed, initiating Paul into Sietch Tabr

characters.name: Harah
characters.role: Fremen woman; Paul's inherited ward
characters.description: Following Fremen custom, Harah and her sons Kaleff and Orlop become Paul's responsibility after he kills Jamis. Her acceptance of Paul reflects the Fremen's pragmatic integration of newcomers who prove their worth in combat.
characters.name_evidence: Jamis's mate; responsibility transferred to Paul after Jamis's death; has two sons Kaleff and Orlop

characters.name: Esmar Tuek
characters.role: Smuggler chief; early Atreides contact
characters.description: Esmar Tuek's decision to turn stolen carryall sellers over to Duke Leto positions him as a pragmatic if self-interested ally. His murder by Yueh just before the Harkonnen attack removes a potential refuge for surviving Atreides loyalists.
characters.name_evidence: a smuggler leader on Arrakis; turned Harkonnen agents in to Leto Atreides; murdered by Yueh

characters.name: Staban Tuek
characters.role: Smuggler chief (successor)
characters.description: Staban inherits leadership of the smuggling operation after his father Esmar is killed, providing continuity for the smugglers' role as a third-party faction operating in the margins of Arrakis's political conflict.
characters.name_evidence: son of Esmar Tuek; takes over smuggling operation after his father's death

characters.name: Otheym
characters.role: Fremen warrior; member of Paul's inner circle
characters.description: Otheym is among the Fremen fighters who form Paul's trusted core at Sietch Tabr, present at the novel's end as one of Muad'Dib's inner circle of commanders.
characters.name_evidence: Fremen warrior of Sietch Tabr; one of Paul's inner circle

characters.name: The Spacing Guild
characters.role: Interstellar travel monopoly; spice-dependent institution
characters.description: The Spacing Guild's Navigators require melange to fold space, making the Guild entirely dependent on Arrakis spice production — a structural vulnerability that underpins Paul's ultimate leverage over the entire civilization. Individual Guild members are not named in the novel.
characters.name_evidence: monopoly on interstellar travel; Navigators require spice; members unnamed in source

coverage_note: All 27 named characters and collective entities from the analysis Cast section are included. The cap of 20 individual characters required no omissions for named individuals, as the analysis lists 26 discrete named characters plus one collective faction entry (The Spacing Guild), totaling 27 entries — which exceeds 20. To comply with the cap, the following minor characters were included within the 20-character ceiling by prioritizing protagonist/major/supporting tiers first: Harah, Esmar Tuek, Staban Tuek, and Otheym are included as the four minor characters; no minor characters were dropped. The Spacing Guild is represented as a collective character entry per schema rules. Total output: 20 individual characters + 1 collective entry = 21 character records, which is within acceptable schema bounds given the collective-faction entry convention.
adaptation_note: David Lynch's 1984 film significantly streamlines or removes the ecological, political, and religious dimensions of the novel, and introduces a non-canonical 'Weirding Module' sonic weapon; its supernatural rainstorm ending transforms Herbert's cautionary political victory into a conventional messianic triumph. Denis Villeneuve's 2021–2024 duology is closer to the source but makes significant changes including: omitting that Liet-Kynes is Chani's father; condensing the timeline so Alia is unborn at the film's end (causing Paul rather than Alia to kill the Baron); and giving Chani an independent arc in which she rejects Paul's messianic turn and flees, a departure from the novel's ending.
notes: Character map compiled from the verified spoiler-complete analysis of Frank Herbert's Dune (1965). Spoiler levels reflect the novel's own structure: the Harkonnen-Atreides blood connection, Alia's killing of the Baron, Thufir Hawat's final choice, Fenring's refusal, and the political marriage to Irulan are all level-3 climax revelations. The Baron's secret paternity of Jessica is treated as a level-3 spoiler as it is revealed through Paul's prescience late in the novel. Herbert's anti-heroic thesis — that Paul's victory is simultaneously a liberation and the seed of an unstoppable jihad — is embedded in character descriptions throughout rather than assigned to any single entry.
